display_title: Decomposition serves as improving the inference efficiency of Transformers

content.comment: Thanks for the pointers to these recent papers that use intra- and inter-attention techniques. Indeed similar ideas have been used in the QA community in the past to model self- and co-attention (c.f. Dynamic Co-attention [Xiong et al., ICLR'17], and Multi-Granularity Hierarchical Attention [Wang et al, ACL'18]). Our goal in this work is not in improving intra- or cross- attention models themselves but to improve efficiency in large Transformers. Our decomposition idea indeed uses the notion of intra- and inter- attention between input elements in but only in service of improving parallelism and cacheability of the compute.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
In this paper, the authors proposed an opinion that it may not be necessary to apply the sequence-wide self-attention over all layers in the BERT model. They proposed a decomposition to a pre-trained Transformer that allows the lower layers to process segments of the input independently, enabling parallelism and caching. The experimental results show that decomposition enables faster inference, significant memory reduction while retaining most of the original performance. 

I think the study problem in this paper is very meaningful. However, this paper has some syntax errors. I hope the author can read their paper carefully and correct grammatical mistakes. 

Questions:
In Figure 2, the authors show the average variance of passage representations when paired with different questions at different layers. But I don’t understand why the variance of the lower layer is smaller than, the higher one. Would the authors like to provide some explanations?
The authors mentioned that the information loss in the lower layers can be potentially compensated for by the higher layers. Would the authors like to provide some theoretical proof and experimental proof?
The authors used the Bayesian Optimization to tune the hyperparameters \gamma, \alpha, and \beta, however, they don’t post the results of the \gamma, \alpha, and \beta in the experimental results. 
In section 4.2, the authors said the search range is [0.1, 2.0] for the 3 hyper-parameters, which confuses me?
In Table 1, would the authors like to explain why the model performs differently in different datasets? Why in the QQP, the model achieves 2.0x Inference Speedup, while it achieves higher Inference Speedup in other datasets?

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer #3
content.comment:
Thanks for your feedback. 

Point 1:
"In Figure 2, the authors show the average variance of passage representations when paired with different questions at different layers. But I don’t understand why the variance of the lower layer is smaller than, the higher one. Would the authors like to provide some explanations?"

Response 1:
Figure 2 aims to answer the following question: Is attention from question tokens important for forming passing representations in the lower layers ( as compared to lower layers)? If this is not the case then we can expect to decompose the attention in lower layers and only use full attention in the upper layers. To answer the question, we measured how the passage representation changes when paired with different questions. If the representation does not change too much (i.e. has low variance) then attention from question tokens is not as important in lower layers. We find that the variance is small in lower layers, meaning that the passage is using more local context before attending to questions in these layers. This empirical observation provides the basic motivation for our decomposition idea.

Point 2:
"The authors mentioned that the information loss in the lower layers can be potentially compensated for by the higher layers. Would the authors like to provide some theoretical proof and experimental proof?"

Response 2:
By compensation, we mean that QA accuracy recovers with fine-tuning and distillation losses. While a theoretical proof might be difficult, it will be interesting to empirically understand how the decomposed model recovers -- whether it learns to recover some of the information that was originally computed in the lower layers or if it learns to work more effectively with the reduced information that is coming from the decomposed lower layers.

Point 3:
"The authors used the Bayesian Optimization to tune the hyperparameters \gamma, \alpha, and \beta, however, they don’t post the results of the \gamma, \alpha, and \beta in the experimental results. 
In section 4.2, the authors said the search range is [0.1, 2.0] for the 3 hyper-parameters, which confuses me?"

Response 3:
The hyper-parameters were obtained using Bayesian Optimization with a search range (i.e, the range of values that the optimizer will search through) [0.1, 2.0]. We will add the final hyperparameters settings to the appendix. 

Point 4:
"In Table 1, would the authors like to explain why the model performs differently in different datasets? Why in the QQP, the model achieves 2.0x Inference Speedup, while it achieves higher Inference Speedup in other datasets?"

Response 4:
The model performance will depend on the size of the cacheable input in the pairwise tasks. In the QA task the cacheable input, the passages, are 11.6x longer (on average, 116 words per passage vs 10 words per question for SQuAD dataset), whereas, in QQP, the cacheable input is similar in size to the other input. This difference in sizes explains the difference in observed inference speedup.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
The paper proposes a way of reducing the computation of pre-trained Transformer models by splitting the lower layers into two parts: one corresponding to a question and one corresponding a passage. Auxiliary losses are added during the fine-tuning stage to recover the lost performance due to the split. While this method alone cannot bring more than 2x speed-up, the authors show that caching of question part when it has to be compared to multiple passages can bring additional saving in computation time. 

The paper is well written and it was easy to understand. It has thorough experiments showing the benefit of the proposed method.

However, I am doubtful of the impact of this paper. The original problem domain is quite limited and it’s not clear if the method would be useful in other scenarios. The method is only relevant when one is using a pre-trained transformer model on two part inputs, and also one part is often have to be compared to multiple other parts. I think the paper can be made stronger by showing the method can be generalized and used in more diverse scenarios.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer #2
content.comment:
Thanks for your feedback. 

"The paper is well written and it was easy to understand. It has thorough experiments showing the benefit of the proposed method. However, I am doubtful of the impact of this paper. The original problem domain is quite limited and it’s not clear if the method would be useful in other scenarios. The method is only relevant when one is using a pre-trained transformer model on two part inputs, and also one part is often have to be compared to multiple other parts. I think the paper can be made stronger by showing the method can be generalized and used in more diverse scenarios."

Response:

In resource-constrained settings such as mobile devices, there are no good solutions to run large models for QA, a key problem in NLP, and other tasks (listed in Section 3 and 4) where one part is to be compared with other parts. Indeed, the main impact of this paper is in showing that decomposition + caching can significantly reduce compute and memory for running such applications mobile devices. 

As for the generalizability of the decomposition idea to other tasks, the underlying motivation behind our decomposition is that local context may be enough in lower layers -- the technique is applicable to any class of NLP problems where this is likely true. Pursuing the idea for other types of tasks is beyond our current scope.

content.title: Official Blind Review #4
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
In this paper, a simple decomposition for transformer models is proposed to speed up the computation for a specific type of problems, where the input has paired, such as a question and an answer for QA tasks. The basic idea is to encode the question and the answer with self-attention alone, and then apply the co-attention on top of them, so that the complexity is reduced from O(p+q)^2 to O(p^2+q^2). Such a decomposed transformer is trained by distilling from a full transformer, where the knowledge distillation loss, layerwise similarity loss and task loss are adopted as the objective functions. Empirical studies show that the proposed method can be up to 3.5 times faster than the full transformer (BERT) model, while only losing a small amount of accuracy.

1. The paper lacks a large body of related and representative works in machine reading comprehension, where such a decomposition is widely used, such as BIDAF (Seo et al.), QANet (Yu et al.), R-Net (Wang et al.) among many others. If those works are properly acknowledged, the novelty in this paper will become slim.

2. The improvement from O(p+q)^2 to O(p^2+q^2) is negligible. On one hand, they are of the same order, so there is no theoretical contribution. On the other, as the author acknowledges, the method can only work on pair-input tasks like QA. However, most of the questions in QA are quite short, so the terms related to q can be ignored and the only bottleneck is p^2, making the difference very minor.

3. Since the method is essentially a distillation, the full transformer model is still needed for supervision. That is to say, it cannot work without the original large model.

4. There are many ways for distillation. For example, one can just use smaller hidden size or a shallower network, or their combinations. Those are straightforward baselines but they are not mentioned or compared with in the paper.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer #4
content.comment:
Thanks for your feedback. 

Point 1: 
"1. The paper lacks a large body of related and representative works in machine reading comprehension, where such a decomposition is widely used, such as BIDAF (Seo et al.), QANet (Yu et al.), R-Net (Wang et al.) among many others. If those works are properly acknowledged, the novelty in this paper will become slim."

Response 1: 
Building decomposable representations is indeed not new. BIDAF (Seo et al.), QANet (Yu et al.), R-Net (Wang et al.) were originally designed as decomposed neural architectures that process question and passage independently in lower layers and use cross attention in upper layers. 

However, large pre-trained transformer models, which are SOTA for many NLP tasks today, are not decomposable by design. The focus of our work is to show that such pre-trained models can be decomposed at the fine-tuning stage to enable caching. Importantly, we show that decomposition + caching enables faster (3x speedup) and low-memory footprint inference (70% less memory) while retaining most of the original models' accuracy (up to 98%).

Point 2: 
"The improvement from O(p+q)^2 to O(p^2+q^2) is negligible. On one hand, they are of the same order, so there is no theoretical contribution. On the other, as the author acknowledges, the method can only work on pair-input tasks like QA. However, most of the questions in QA are quite short, so the terms related to q can be ignored and the only bottleneck is p^2, making the difference very minor."

Response 2: 
Decomposition enables caching of passage representations. This means runtime actually reduces from O(p+q)^2 to O(c + q^2), a substantial speedup. c is a constant depends on the lookup time for cached representations. As the reviewer points out decomposition also reduces runtime compute from O(p+q)^2 to O(p^2+q^2), even without caching. However, this compute reduction is significant only when p and q are of comparable sizes, making the O(2pq) = O(p^2). To reiterate, we have shown that decomposition yields significant inference speedup, going from O(p+q)^2 to O(c + q^2) for tasks like QA.

Point 3: 
"Since the method is essentially a distillation, the full transformer model is still needed for supervision. That is to say, it cannot work without the original large model."

Response 3:
Our method is not distillation alone. In fact, we showed that simple decomposition during fine-tuning with caching without any distillation loss for fine-tuning itself brings the majority of the speedup we are getting at a very low cost of accuracy drop. We only use a distillation-style loss to further reduce the accuracy loss. 

As to the need for the original large model, it fits in well with our main goal: To take pre-trained transformer models and modify them to enable faster inference with reduced memory footprint. This is not a limitation since we are not proposing a new transformer architecture that is trained from scratch.

Point 4:
"There are many ways for distillation. For example, one can just use smaller hidden size or a shallower network, or their combinations. Those are straightforward baselines but they are not mentioned or compared with in the paper. "

Response 4:
Our related work section discusses the applicability of techniques that use model compression with distillation. 

The main point is that different from model compression ideas, our approach retains much of the large model capacities of pre-trained transformers, a key reason for their success. We obtain faster inference by enabling parallel processing and caching of segments. In this vein, our approach is orthogonal to compression/distillation methods. As indirect evidence, we have shown in the experiments that the decomposed BERT-large model even runs faster than BERT-base, which could be seen as a form distilled BERT-large, and yet gives better accuracy than BERT-base.

As for empirical comparison, the only known result at the time of our submission was DistillBERT. Our work outperforms DistillBERT (which is only 1.6x faster and has 3.5 points accuracy drop on SQuAD, whereas our decomposed BERT runs 3.2x faster and has 1.4 points drop). There are concurrent research works [e.g. TinyBERT, Compressing BERT, that are under submission at ICLR’20] on compressing BERT or distilling BERT models, but how to apply compression for pre-trained transformers like BERT is still a non-trivial and challenging open problem.
